mcqs.q: The main organ of drug metabolism is the:
mcqs.explain: Drugs are metabolised mainly in the liver (and to a lesser extent lungs, kidneys, blood and intestines).

mcqs.q: For a lipophilic drug to be EXCRETED, metabolism must make it:
mcqs.explain: Lipophilic drugs are reabsorbed in the tubules; they must be made hydrophilic to be excreted in urine.

mcqs.q: Phase I reactions are mainly catalysed by:
mcqs.explain: Phase I oxidation/reduction/hydrolysis is catalysed by the cytochrome P450 system (microsomal mixed-function oxidase), e.g. CYP3A4, CYP2D6.

mcqs.q: Phase II metabolism consists of:
mcqs.explain: Phase II is conjugation with glucuronic acid, sulfate, acetate or amino acids, producing polar, water-soluble, usually inactive metabolites.

mcqs.q: The metabolites produced by Phase II conjugation are usually:
mcqs.explain: Conjugation gives polar, water-soluble compounds that are most often therapeutically inactive and readily excreted.

mcqs.q: Microsomal enzymes (the CYPs) are located on the smooth ER and are:
opts: Identical in all individuals with no variation
mcqs.explain: Microsomal enzymes (mainly hepatic) sit on the smooth endoplasmic reticulum and are inducible by drugs and diet.

mcqs.q: Non-microsomal enzymes (esterases, amidases) are:
opts: Not inducible but show genetic polymorphism
mcqs.explain: Non-microsomal enzymes are in cytoplasm, mitochondria and plasma; they are not inducible but exhibit polymorphism.

mcqs.q: Drugs are PRIMARILY excreted by the:
mcqs.explain: The kidneys are the primary route of excretion; other routes include bile, intestine, lung and breast milk.

mcqs.q: The renal handling of a drug involves:
opts: Glomerular filtration, active secretion and tubular reabsorption
mcqs.explain: Renal elimination = glomerular filtration, active tubular secretion, and passive reabsorption of lipid-soluble un-ionized drug.

mcqs.q: In the distal tubule, which form of a drug is REABSORBED rather than excreted?
mcqs.explain: Lipid-soluble un-ionized drug is passively reabsorbed; ionized/polar metabolites are trapped and excreted in urine.

mcqs.q: Acidification of the urine will:
opts: Increase reabsorption (and decrease excretion) of weak acids
Have no effect on weak acids
mcqs.explain: Acidic urine keeps weak acids un-ionized, increasing their reabsorption and reducing excretion; alkalinization has the opposite effect.

mcqs.q: An elderly patient with reduced renal function is most at risk of toxicity from:
opts: Narrow-therapeutic-range drugs excreted renally, such as digoxin
Drugs with a wide safety margin
mcqs.explain: Reduced renal clearance lets renally-excreted, narrow-window drugs (e.g. digoxin, sotalol) accumulate to toxic levels.

mcqs.q: Ampicillin is a good choice for a biliary-tract infection because it:
opts: Is excreted in high concentrations in the bile
Is only excreted by the kidney
mcqs.explain: Ampicillin is excreted in high concentrations in bile, making it effective against biliary-tract infections — excretion influences prescribing.

mcqs.q: The half-life (t½) of a drug is the time for the plasma concentration to:
opts: Fall to one-half of its value
mcqs.explain: Half-life is the time required for the plasma drug concentration to decrease by one-half of its initial value.

mcqs.q: Which drug has the LONGEST half-life of the following?
mcqs.explain: Digoxin's half-life is ~36 h, far longer than aspirin (~6 h) or metronidazole (~9 h).

mcqs.q: A SHORT half-life is associated with:
opts: Extensive tissue uptake, rapid metabolism and rapid excretion
Extensive protein binding and slow metabolism
mcqs.explain: Short half-life follows extensive tissue uptake, rapid metabolism and rapid excretion; long half-life follows protein binding, slow metabolism, poor excretion.

mcqs.q: In theory, the optimal dosing interval is approximately equal to the:
mcqs.explain: Ideally the dose interval equals the half-life; too long fails to maintain effect, too short risks toxicity.

mcqs.q: A loading dose is used to:
opts: Quickly achieve a high therapeutic concentration (≈ twice the maintenance dose)
mcqs.explain: A loading dose (about twice the maintenance dose) rapidly raises the drug to therapeutic concentrations when the condition demands it.

mcqs.q: A drug with extensive protein binding and slow metabolism will tend to have a:
mcqs.explain: Extensive protein binding, slow metabolism and poor excretion all prolong the half-life.

mcqs.q: Why can the kidney NOT efficiently eliminate highly lipophilic drugs?
opts: They readily cross membranes and are reabsorbed in the distal tubule
They are too large to be filtered
mcqs.explain: Lipophilic drugs cross cell membranes and are reabsorbed from the tubule, so they must first be metabolised to water-soluble forms.

mcqs.q: A patient in renal failure may have drugs removed by:
opts: Dialysis (which removes small molecules such as drugs)
mcqs.explain: Dialysis removes small molecules including many drugs, useful when renal excretion fails.

mcqs.q: Metabolic rate is important because it determines the:
opts: Duration of the drug's action (and dosing frequency)
mcqs.explain: How fast a drug is metabolised sets the duration of its action, which in turn dictates how often it must be given.

saqs.q: Differentiate Phase I and Phase II metabolism.
saqs.a: Phase I: oxidation/reduction/hydrolysis by cytochrome P450. Phase II: conjugation (glucuronic acid, sulfate, etc.) giving polar, water-soluble, usually inactive metabolites.
Microsomal (smooth ER, mainly liver) — inducible by drugs/diet (CYPs). Non-microsomal (cytoplasm/mitochondria/plasma) — not inducible but polymorphic (esterases, amidases).

saqs.q: List the routes of drug excretion.
saqs.a: Mainly the kidneys; also bile, intestine, lung and breast milk. Drugs must be hydrophilic to be excreted.

saqs.q: How does urinary pH affect drug excretion?
saqs.a: Acidic urine increases reabsorption (decreases excretion) of weak acids; alkaline urine increases their excretion. The reverse applies to weak bases.

saqs.q: Define half-life and relate it to dose interval.
saqs.a: Half-life (t½) = time for the plasma concentration to fall by half. The ideal dose interval ≈ the half-life (too long = sub-therapeutic, too short = toxicity).

saqs.q: What determines a short vs a long half-life?
saqs.a: Short: extensive tissue uptake, rapid metabolism, rapid excretion. Long: extensive protein binding, slow metabolism, poor excretion.

saqs.q: What is a loading dose and when is it used?
saqs.a: An initial dose (≈ twice the maintenance dose) used when the condition demands high concentrations quickly.
